summary: Describes the IS-IS extensions needed for Segment Routing running on an MPLS data plane. IS-IS advertises the segments that let flexible end-to-end paths be built as sequences of topological subpaths.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC is the IS-IS counterpart of the OSPF segment routing extensions. It defines the small boxes that IS-IS routers add to their link-state advertisements so that every router learns which numbers it can use for prefixes, which for links, and which block of labels it keeps for itself.

what is the sid label binding tlv
subtitle: How IS-IS routers advertise the identifiers and label ranges that Segment Routing over MPLS relies on.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing builds paths from segments, so every router needs a way to tell the others which segment identifiers it has and which MPLS label ranges it uses.
tldr.mechanism: IS-IS gets new sub-TLVs for Prefix-SIDs, Adjacency SIDs and LAN Adjacency SIDs, two new Binding TLVs for mapping prefixes to SIDs, and new Router Capability sub-TLVs for label ranges and algorithms.
tldr.outcome: SR paths over MPLS then need no LDP or RSVP-TE signaling, only the regular IGP. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8667 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2019. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updating it. The RFC says IS-IS now carries information used to program the MPLS data plane, so the same attacks that can be carried out on the IP control plane can also misroute label-switched traffic.

sections.title: What These Extensions Add
sections.content:
Segment Routing allows for a flexible definition of end-to-end paths within IGP topologies by encoding paths as sequences of topological sub-paths called segments. These segments are advertised by the link-state routing protocols, IS-IS and OSPF. Prefix segments represent an ECMP-aware shortest path to a prefix or a node, as per the state of the IGP topology. Adjacency segments represent a hop over a specific adjacency between two nodes in the IGP. A prefix segment is typically a multi-hop path, while an adjacency segment is in most cases a one-hop path.

SR's control plane can be applied to both IPv6 and MPLS data planes and does not require any additional signaling other than the regular IGP. For example, when used in MPLS networks, SR paths do not require any LDP or RSVP-TE signaling, though SR can interoperate in the presence of Label Switched Paths established with RSVP or LDP. There are additional segment types, for example the Binding SID defined in RFC 8402, and this document also defines an advertisement for one type of Binding SID, the Mirror Context segment.

The document describes the IS-IS extensions that need to be introduced for Segment Routing operating on an MPLS data plane. The Segment Routing architecture is described in RFC 8402 and its use cases in RFC 7855.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is small but far-reaching: the routing protocol that already tells routers about the network topology now also tells them which labels and shortcuts they may use.

sections.title: The Identifiers Defined Here
sections.content:
The Segment Routing architecture defines different types of Segment Identifiers. This document defines the IS-IS encodings for the IGP-Prefix Segment, the IGP-Adjacency Segment, the IGP-LAN-Adjacency Segment and the Binding Segment.

The Prefix Segment Identifier sub-TLV carries the IGP-Prefix-SID, and the Prefix-SID MUST be unique within a given IGP domain when the L-Flag is not set. A Prefix-SID sub-TLV is associated with a prefix advertised by a node and MAY be present in the TLV-135 Extended IPv4 reachability TLV, the TLV-235 Multi-topology IPv4 Reachability TLV, the TLV-236 IPv6 IP Reachability TLV and the TLV-237 Multi-topology IPv6 IP Reachability TLV, as well as in the Binding TLV and the Multi-Topology Binding TLV defined in the same document.

The Adjacency Segment Identifier sub-TLV is an optional sub-TLV carrying the IGP-Adjacency-SID, with flags and fields that may in future extensions carry other types of SIDs. IS-IS adjacencies are advertised using the IS Neighbor TLVs: TLV-22 Extended IS reachability, TLV-222 MT-ISN, TLV-23 IS Neighbor Attribute, TLV-223 MT IS Neighbor Attribute, and TLV-141 inter-AS reachability information. Multiple Adj-SID sub-TLVs MAY be associated with a single IS Neighbor.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of shortcut are advertised: one that stands for a whole path to an address, one that stands for a single link, and one that stands for a link on a shared LAN.

sections.title: The Prefix-SID Sub-TLV and Its Flags
sections.content:
The Prefix-SID sub-TLV has Type 3 and a Length of 5 or 6 octets depending on the size of the SID. It carries a Flags octet, an Algorithm octet and the SID, Index or Label field. The Algorithm field holds the identifier of the algorithm the router uses to compute the reachability of the prefix, and at origination it MUST be set to 0 or to a value advertised in the SR-Algorithm sub-TLV. A router receiving a Prefix-SID from a remote node with an algorithm value that node has not advertised MUST ignore the sub-TLV.

The flags carry several separate meanings. The R-Flag, Re-advertisement, says the prefix has been propagated by the router from another level or by redistribution, and it MUST be set for prefixes that are not local to the router and are advertised because of propagation, leaking or redistribution. The N-Flag, Node-SID, says the Prefix-SID refers to the router identified by the prefix, and it is typically set on Prefix-SIDs attached to a router loopback address. A router MAY set the N-Flag only if the prefix is local to the router and has a prefix length of either /32 for IPv4 or /128 for IPv6.

The P-Flag, No Penultimate Hop-Popping, means the penultimate hop MUST NOT pop the Prefix-SID before delivering the packet to the node that advertised it. The E-Flag, Explicit NULL, means any upstream neighbour of the originator MUST replace the Prefix-SID with one that has an Explicit NULL value, 0 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6. The V-Flag says whether the Prefix-SID carries a value instead of an index, and the L-Flag says whether that value or index has local rather than global significance; by default both are unset. Other bits MUST be zero when originated and ignored when received.

When the V-Flag and L-Flag are both 0, the SID/Index/Label field is a 4-octet index defining the offset in the SID/Label space advertised by the router. When both are 1, it is a 3-octet local label where the 20 rightmost bits are used. All other combinations are invalid and any advertisement received with an invalid setting MUST be ignored.

When the P-Flag is not set, any upstream neighbour MUST pop the Prefix-SID, which is the penultimate hop-popping mechanism of the MPLS data plane, and the received E-Flag is ignored. When the P-Flag is set and the E-Flag is not, the neighbour MUST keep the Prefix-SID on top of the stack, which is useful when the originator has to stitch the packet into a continuing LSP. When both are set, the neighbour MUST replace the Prefix-SID with one having an Explicit NULL value, which is useful when the originator is the final destination and wants the original EXP bits. When propagating a reachability advertisement originated by another IS-IS speaker, the router MUST set the P-Flag and MUST clear the E-Flag. The Prefix-SID sub-TLV MUST be included when the associated Prefix Reachability TLV is propagated across level boundaries, and the Level-1-2 router that propagates it maintains the content, flags and SID, except for the rules above.
sections.plainLanguage: The flags tell the other routers how to handle the packet when it arrives with that identifier on top. Should the neighbour remove it before the last hop, keep it, or replace it with an empty label? Should the identifier mean this router or the network at large?

sections.title: Adjacency and LAN Adjacency Identifiers
sections.content:
The Adj-SID sub-TLV has Type 31 and a Length of 5 or 6 octets depending on the size of the SID. It carries a Flags octet, a Weight octet for load balancing, and the SID, Label or Index field.

The F-Flag is the Address-Family flag: when it is unset the Adj-SID is used when forwarding IPv4-encapsulated traffic to the neighbour, and when it is set it is used for IPv6-encapsulated traffic, so the router advertises the outgoing encapsulation of the adjacency. The B-Flag marks an Adj-SID that is eligible for protection, for example by IP Fast Reroute or MPLS Fast Reroute. The V-Flag says the Adj-SID carries a value and the L-Flag says the value has local significance; by default both are set for an Adj-SID. The S-Flag, Set flag, indicates that the Adj-SID refers to a set of adjacencies and may therefore be assigned to other adjacencies as well. The P-Flag, Persistent, means the value remains consistent across a router restart or an interface flap. When the P-Flag is not set the Adj-SID MAY be persistent, and when it is set it MUST be persistent.

In LAN subnetworks the Designated Intermediate System is elected and originates the Pseudonode LSP including all neighbours of the DIS. When Segment Routing is used, each router in the LAN MAY advertise the Adj-SID of each of its neighbours. Since on a LAN each router advertises only one adjacency, to the DIS, the router advertises the set of Adj-SIDs for each of its LAN neighbours inside a newly defined sub-TLV that is part of the TLV advertising the adjacency to the DIS, such as TLV-22.

The LAN-Adj-SID sub-TLV has Type 32 and a variable Length. It carries the same flags as the Adj-SID sub-TLV, a Weight octet, the IS-IS System-ID of the neighbour for which the Adj-SID is advertised, of the length defined as ID Length in ISO 10589, and the SID, Label or Index field. Multiple LAN-Adj-SID sub-TLVs MAY be encoded, and the sub-TLV MUST NOT appear in TLV 141. If the adjacency to the DIS cannot carry the whole set of LAN-Adj-SID sub-TLVs, multiple advertisements of that adjacency MUST be used and all of them MUST have the same metric.
sections.plainLanguage: An adjacency identifier names one link. On a shared LAN, where routers are all wired together, each router lists the identifiers it assigned to each of its neighbours, so that anyone in the level can work out the shape of the LAN and the labels on it.

sections.title: The SID/Label Binding TLV
sections.content:
The SID/Label Binding TLV MAY be originated by any router in an IS-IS domain. It has Type 149 and a variable Length, and it may be used to advertise prefix to SID/Label mappings, which is the Segment Routing Mapping Server functionality defined in RFC 8661. It may also be used to advertise a Mirror SID, indicating the ability of a node to process traffic originally destined to another IGP node.

The TLV carries a Flags octet, a RESERVED octet, a 2-octet Range, a Prefix Length octet, the Prefix of 0 to 16 octets, and sub-TLVs. The F-Flag says whether the prefix is IPv4 or IPv6. The M-Flag, Mirror Context, is set when the advertised SID corresponds to a mirrored context. The S-Flag says the TLV SHOULD be flooded across the entire routing domain; if it is not set the TLV MUST NOT be leaked between levels, and this bit MUST NOT be altered during leaking. The D-Flag MUST be set when the TLV is leaked from Level-2 to Level-1, and MUST be clear otherwise, to prevent looping across levels. The A-Flag, Attached, may be set by the originator to signal that the prefixes and SIDs are directly connected to it, and it MUST be cleared if the TLV is leaked to other areas or levels.

The Range field lets a router specify a range of addresses and their associated Prefix-SIDs, which is a compression scheme for distributing a continuous prefix and its continuous SID or Label block. If a single SID is advertised, the Range MUST be set to one, and for larger advertisements it MUST be the number of addresses to be mapped. In either case the prefix is the first address to which a SID is assigned. Only the most significant octets of the prefix are encoded, from 1 octet for a prefix length of up to 8 up to 16 octets for a prefix length of up to 128.

The Prefix-SID sub-TLV MUST be present in the SID/Label Binding TLV when the M-Flag is clear, and MUST NOT be present when the M-Flag is set, in which case the SID/Label sub-TLV is present instead. Because it is not expected that an operator can keep fully continuous Prefix, SID and Index mappings, an implementation MAY generate several instances of the Binding TLV to cover non-continuous ranges. The RFC's example shows three ranges, of 16, 6 and 41 addresses, needing three instances.
sections.plainLanguage: This TLV is how a controller hands out identifiers for addresses it manages. It can cover a whole block of addresses in one advertisement, and it can also say that a node is able to stand in for another node.

sections.title: What a Router Advertises About Itself
sections.content:
Segment Routing requires each router to advertise its SR data plane capability and the range of MPLS label values it uses for Segment Routing when global SIDs are allocated. Data plane capabilities and label ranges are advertised with the SR-Capabilities sub-TLV, which is inserted into the IS-IS Router Capability TLV defined in RFC 7981. The SR-Capabilities sub-TLV MUST be propagated throughout the level and MUST NOT be advertised across level boundaries, so the S-Flag in the Router Capability TLV MUST be unset.

The SR-Capabilities sub-TLV has Type 2 and a variable Length. Its Flags octet holds the I-Flag, the MPLS IPv4 flag, set when the router can process SR-MPLS-encapsulated IPv4 packets on all interfaces, and the V-Flag, the MPLS IPv6 flag. It then carries one or more Segment Routing Global Block descriptor entries, each with a 3-octet Range and a SID/Label sub-TLV holding the first value of the block, where the range value MUST be higher than 0.

When multiple descriptors are advertised, the entries define an ordered set of ranges on which a SID index is applied, so changing the advertised order has a disruptive effect on forwarding. A new descriptor SHOULD be added at the end of the sub-TLV without changing the order of previously advertised blocks, since reordering creates label churn in the forwarding table and can black-hole traffic during convergence. The originating router MUST ensure the order is unchanged after a graceful restart and MUST NOT advertise overlapping ranges. The RFC's example shows ranges of 100 starting at 100, 1000 and 500, which receiving routers concatenate in the received order to build the SRGB.

The SR-Algorithm sub-TLV, of Type 19, advertises the algorithms the router is currently using, with values taken from the IGP Algorithm Type registry defined in RFC 8665: algorithm 0 is the shortest path algorithm on link metric, which permits any node to overwrite the path with a different one based on local policy, and algorithm 1 is the strict version, which requires all nodes along the path to honour the routing decision. When the originating router does not advertise the sub-TLV, algorithm 0 is the only algorithm supported.

The SR Local Block sub-TLV, of Type 22, contains the range of labels the node has reserved for Local SIDs, which are used for example for Adj-SIDs and may also be allocated by components other than IS-IS, such as an application or a controller instructing the router to allocate a specific Local SID. The SRMS Preference sub-TLV advertises a preference value for the node acting as an SR Mapping Server.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anyone can build a path, every router has to say what it is able to do and which labels it has set aside for itself. The order of those label blocks matters, because it is what turns an index into a label.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: With the use of the extensions defined in this document, IS-IS carries information that will be used to program the MPLS data plane. In general, the same type of attacks that can be carried out on the IP/IPv6 control plane can be carried out on the MPLS control plane, resulting in traffic being misrouted in the respective data planes, and the latter may be more difficult to detect and isolate. Existing security extensions as described in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 apply to these Segment Routing extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Because IS-IS now also steers label-switched traffic, an attacker who can inject advertisements can misroute that traffic as well as the ordinary IP traffic, and doing so may be harder to spot.

items.title: R-Flag
items.text: Re-advertisement: the prefix was propagated from another level or redistributed.

items.title: N-Flag
items.text: Node-SID: the identifier refers to the router, usually set on a loopback prefix.

items.title: P-Flag
items.text: No Penultimate Hop-Popping: the neighbour keeps the SID on the stack.

items.title: E-Flag
items.text: Explicit NULL: the neighbour replaces the SID with an Explicit NULL value.

items.title: V-Flag
items.text: The SID carries a value rather than an index.

items.title: L-Flag
items.text: The value or index has local rather than global significance.

viz.caption: HOW THE SID VALUE IS READ

cells: A 4-octet index giving the offset in the router's advertised SID space
A 3-octet local label, with the 20 rightmost bits used for the label value
Invalid; the advertisement must be ignored

viz.caption: THE FLAGS OF AN ADJ-SID SUB-TLV

items.title: F-Flag
items.text: Address family: the Adj-SID is used for IPv6 rather than IPv4 traffic.

items.title: B-Flag
items.text: Backup: the adjacency is eligible for protection by fast reroute.

items.title: V-Flag
items.text: The Adj-SID carries a value; set by default.

items.title: L-Flag
items.text: The value has local significance; set by default.

items.title: S-Flag
items.text: Set: the Adj-SID refers to a set of adjacencies.

items.title: P-Flag
items.text: Persistent: the value survives a restart or an interface flap.
